label: Wheeled Mobile Robots
notes: This chapter studies how wheel design decides which chassis velocities a planar robot can command. We separate omnidirectional bases, which span every planar twist directly, from nonholonomic bases, whose rolling constraints forbid instantaneous sideways motion yet still reach any pose by maneuvering.

label: The Chassis Lives in SE(2)
notes: A wheeled robot is read as a planar rigid body whose pose sits in SE(2). The body-frame chassis twist carries yaw rate, forward velocity, and lateral velocity. Naming this twist first lets every wheel model appear as a linear constraint acting on the same three numbers.

label: Wheels as Velocity Constraints
notes: A wheel is not just an actuator; it declares which contact component rolls, which must not slip, and which becomes wheel angular speed. Changing only the wheel modules turns one rectangular chassis into several different robots, so we always read wheels as constraints on the chassis twist.

label: The Unicycle Model
notes: The unicycle is the canonical nonholonomic base. It commands forward speed and turning rate, while its body-sideways velocity is pinned to zero at every instant. Integrating these controls rotates forward motion through the heading, so curved paths still accumulate world-frame lateral displacement.

label: Differential Drive and the Car
notes: Differential drive sets forward speed and yaw rate from two wheel speeds, recovering the unicycle twist. The car-like robot adds a steering angle and a wheelbase, so curvature is bounded. Both share the no-side-slip rolling constraint that defines nonholonomic motion.

label: The Rolling Constraint Is Pfaffian
notes: The no-side-slip condition is a Pfaffian constraint: linear in the velocities but not integrable to a position constraint. That non-integrability is exactly why the configuration space stays three dimensional while only two velocity directions are available at any instant.

label: Omnidirectional Bases
notes: Mecanum and omni wheels add passive rollers that let four wheel speeds span all three planar twist components. The wheel map then has rank three, so a least-squares inverse recovers a commanded chassis twist. No planar direction is missing in the ideal instantaneous kinematic model.

label: The Mecanum Wheel Map
notes: The mecanum matrix H sends the body twist to four wheel rates and depends on length, width, and wheel radius. With rank three the four wheels overconstrain rather than underconstrain motion, and the pseudo-inverse reconstructs compatible twists to floating-point accuracy, which the notebook verifies numerically.

label: Odometry and Dead Reckoning
notes: Odometry integrates the running account of small twist decisions. Each step rotates body-frame motion into the world frame and accumulates heading. Wrong wheel radii, roller angles, or encoder signs quietly amplify into pose drift, so dead reckoning must be checked against both algebra and motion.

label: Controllability and Planning
notes: Even with no sideways velocity, a nonholonomic robot is controllable: Lie brackets of forward and turning motions generate the missing direction. That is why parallel parking needs a maneuver of short alternating moves rather than a single straight slide into the gap.

label: Feedback Control to a Pose
notes: Feedback control steers a nonholonomic base toward a target pose or trajectory using errors in position and heading. Because instantaneous sideways motion is impossible, the controller commands forward speed and yaw rate, letting curvature and heading change resolve the lateral error over time.

label: Mobile Manipulation
notes: Mounting an arm on a mobile base combines base mobility with arm reach through one stacked Jacobian. Redundant degrees of freedom let the end effector follow a task while the base repositions, and nonholonomic base constraints carry directly into the combined velocity map.

label: Recap and Invariants
notes: Mobile robot kinematics is constraint geometry on SE(2). Instantaneous mobility and global reachability are different questions: omnidirectional bases span planar velocity now, nonholonomic bases reach poses by paths. The numerical checks confirm rank three, accurate reconstruction, and a nonzero unicycle path length.
